items.title: Agentic Security and Operating Systems: A Deep Review and Prospectus of OpSec, Cognitive Security, and Agentic Cyber Security
items.summary: AI agents now hold genuine system authority: they execute code, touch credentials, open network egress, parse hostile documents, and in many deployments initiate or approve changes to the very infrastructure they run on.
items.content: Agentic Security and Operating Systems: A Deep Review and Prospectus of OpSec, Cognitive Security, and Agentic Cyber Security Friedman, Daniel Ari Daniel Ari Friedman Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22754351 Friedman2026AgenticSecurityOperatingSystems218 Computational Paper AI agents now hold genuine system authority: they execute code, touch credentials, open network egress, parse hostile documents, and in many deployments initiate or approve changes to the very infrastructure they run on. This review, dated 2026-09-10, examines what that shift does to operating-system security. The primary scenario is a technically capable operator whose workstation faces both **exploitation** — an attacker compromising a browser, parser, dependency, or agent tool and then crossing a boundary — and **authorized misuse** — an attacker persuading an agent to use its existing, legitimate access to exfiltrate secrets or authorize consequential actions. The second path requires no kernel exploit at all, which reframes the evaluation: the axis of analysis is the authority a component already holds, not merely the difficulty of exploiting it. This revision (0.7.0) refreshes the evidence base through September 11, 2026. The offensive baseline expands from four primary sources to the incident record now available: the NCSC assessments of January 2024 and May 2025, the Anthropic campaign investigation of November 2025 — whose tradecraft MITRE has canonized as campaign C0062 — the August 2025 "vibe hacking" report and the September 2026 threat-intelligence report on credential theft, OpenAI's disruption reporting and its October 2025 counterpoint, Google GTIG's analysis of an autonomous credential-harvesting campaign, the OpenAI–Hugging Face evaluation incident of July 2026, the UK AI Security Institute's unsanctioned-behavior incident (nineteen out-of-scope actions across seven models), and DARPA's AIxCC finals, where AI systems identified and patched vulnerabilities, including real, non-synthetic ones, at measured rates. The platform reviews absorb the 2026 record: Qubes 4.3.0 (Xen 4.19, the sys-gui split, the Devices API, the salt management model, and the QSB-118 dom0 injection, CVE-2026-82636) and Nix 2.34/2.35 with its advisory chain, the removal of the hardened profiles, and 95.18 percent measured ISO reproducibility. The analysis is situated against the standards landscape — the OWASP Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations guide and the December 2025 Top 10 for Agentic Applications, CSA's MAESTRO framework, the NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative, and the CISA-led Five-Eyes adoption guidance — and against the convergent sandboxing practice of the major coding agents, which together motivate the OS-level lens this review applies. A defensive-stack matrix (24 candidates against eight mitigation classes) joins the candidate–property matrix as a second deterministic artifact. The review extends the underlying architectural assessment into three domains the source treatment only touches implicitly: **cognitive security** (the authorized-misuse surface, where persuasion substitutes for exploitation), **operator OpSec** (the practices that keep compartmentalization real under workload pressure), and **agent-orchestration security** (the boundary design of multi-agent systems themselves). Deep reviews of Qubes OS and NixOS anchor the analysis. The review ships its concepts in two forms: the prose analysis, and a harness-neutral skill library (a `skills/` registry with conformance tests, following [@cogsecskills2026]) that lets an agent harness apply the evaluation vocabulary, the authority ladder, and the other review concepts directly. The evaluation artifacts — the candidate–property matrix and the defensive-stack matrix — regenerate deterministically from pinned data modules. The work is citable via its Zenodo DOI (printed on the cover). Keywords: agentic security, operating systems, compartmentalization, capability mediation, Qubes OS, NixOS, threat modeling, cognitive security, operational security, agent orchestration, offensive AI, reproducible builds. Source and skills: https://github.com/docxology/agentic_os_security (evaluation layer, skills library, and this manuscript regenerate from pinned data modules). agentic security operating systems compartmentalization capability mediation Qubes OS NixOS cognitive security operational security agent orchestration offensive AI The review argues that delegated legitimate authority, not exploit difficulty, should be the primary evaluation axis for agent-bearing systems. Across the documented agentic incidents reviewed, damage was bounded by a boundary or human gate rather than by model restraint. Qubes is judged to supply the strongest deployable compartmentalization, while NixOS supplies reproducible, auditable operations that are not by themselves confinement. The author notes that three coding-agent vendors independently converged on OS-primitive sandboxing, proxy-mediated egress, and classifier-gated escalation. The prospectus recommends capability mediation layers that make every agent tool call a checked decision made outside the agent. Evaluation of 24 OS candidates against 9 security properties — Qubes, NixOS, hardened desktops, server platforms, privacy systems, non-Linux comparators and offensive distros are each judged on nine properties. Document-based analysis with no penetration testing and no numeric scores — Judgments draw on documented designs, advisories, and primary incident reports; the review explicitly avoids testing and composite scores. Deterministic candidate-property and defensive-stack matrices from pinned data — A companion codebase encodes the 24x9 stance matrix (strong/partial/weak/n_a) and a 24-candidate x 8-mitigation-class matrix, regenerated reproducibly. Two-path threat model: exploitation versus authorized misuse — Frames threats by the authority a component already holds, grounded in a 2024-2026 incident record (NCSC, Anthropic, AISI, OpenAI, DARPA AIxCC). Harness-neutral skill library with conformance tests — Review concepts (stance evaluation, authority ladder, delegation bound, invariants, incident taxonomy) ship as SKILL.md files indexed by a registry.

items.title: Jev in Practice: A Composable Python Toolkit for TypeSafe's System One Decision Model
items.summary: Jev is TypeSafe's flagship System One decision model: instead of generating text, it answers typed questions (Choice, Score, Noul) about a state with calibrated probabilities that software can branch on directly. This wo
items.content: Jev in Practice: A Composable Python Toolkit for TypeSafe's System One Decision Model Friedman, Daniel Ari Daniel Ari Friedman Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22816187 Friedman2026JevPracticeComposablePython219 Computational Paper Jev is TypeSafe's flagship System One decision model: instead of generating text, it answers typed questions (Choice, Score, Noul) about a state with calibrated probabilities that software can branch on directly. This work presents daf-jev, an open, modular, composable Python toolkit for the Jev API, together with a live-API characterization of the model. The package layers ergonomic question builders, a decision-composition library (confidence gates, tiered routing, composite scoring), a concurrent corpus evaluator, a calibration module, a CLI, an agent skill, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server over a thin typed client. Live benchmarks show that batching questions into one call is faster and cheaper than sequential calls (up to ~18x speedup and ~4x fewer tokens), that decision pipelines complete within the model's millisecond envelope, and that reported confidence is self-consistent across repeated evaluations. All numbers in the accompanying manuscript are generated from benchmark artifacts; the full provenance chain (hashed documentation snapshot, figure registry, validation receipts) is machine-checked. Batching questions into one call gave wall-time speedups of 3.98, 8.77, and 18.55 across the configured batch widths. At the widest batch width the sequential strategy used 4.22 times the tokens of the batched call, so batching was both faster and cheaper. End-to-end decision pipelines had median wall times of 0.133 s (composite scoring) and 0.129 s (intent routing). Under a self-consistency proxy, the calibration benchmark reported ECE 0.0730 and Brier 0.0252; the author notes this shows consistency with proxy labels, not correctness about the world. The unit test suite reached 93.08 measured coverage. daf-jev layered Python client for the System One endpoint — Implements typed builders (noul, choice, score), sync/async clients with a pure retry policy, and a typed exception hierarchy over one HTTP endpoint. Pure-function decision patterns and a concurrent batch Evaluator — composite_score, confidence_gate, and route/pick turn typed answers into decisions locally; the Evaluator runs a fixed question set over many states without aborting on failures. Live-API batching benchmark at batch widths 5, 10, and 20 — Compares one batched call against sequential single-question calls on the jev-latest model, recording wall time and token totals. Self-consistency calibration benchmark (6 states × 5 repeats) — Scores choice answers against the modal choice across repeats and noul answers by pairwise stability, computing ECE and Brier score without external ground truth. No-mock test suite and hash-manifested documentation snapshot — Unit tests drive the real transport against a local HTTP server; model claims are grounded in a 108-page hashed snapshot of the vendor documentation.

items.title: Green Line: a capacity-under-development instrument
items.summary: A capacity-under-development instrument: the green line of the docxology line-set. It records what is deliberately still being learned — apprenticeships, skills not yet mastered — with marker/counter-signal staging, and
items.content: Green Line: a capacity-under-development instrument Friedman, Daniel Ari Daniel Ari Friedman Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22833491 Friedman2026GreenLineCapacityUnder220 Computational Paper A capacity-under-development instrument: the green line of the docxology line-set. It records what is deliberately still being learned — apprenticeships, skills not yet mastered — with marker/counter-signal staging, and reads declared growth records against a versioned registry. Observations phrased as certification or credential language are staged aside with a note, never scored. It measures what is still growing — never competence, mastery, or virtue. Code and prose are Apache-2.0 licensed. See LICENSE in the repository. active inference governance apprenticeship growth records capacity under development open science A read returns one of four staged statuses describing marker coverage at a review date, explicitly not competence, mastery or permission. In the worked example, one applied record reads STAGED and the rest NEEDS_MARKER, so the overall status is NEEDS_MARKER. Adding a 'certified as expert' observation leaves the read unchanged because certification language is staged aside rather than scored. The author states the limit that a read describes marker declarations, not verified practice or skill growth. The author notes counter-signal detection is lexical, so an innocently phrased resume-shaped record passes intake. Three-stage read: intake, tag-intersection matching, status projection — Self-declared observations are normalized fail-closed, matched to growth records whose tags intersect the attempt's tags, then projected into present/missing/stale marker surfaces. Formal definitions of growth records, freshness windows and aggregation — Defines growth records, cultivation attempts, freshness relative to a review date and window, a finding rule, and an aggregation rule over four statuses. Lexical counter-signal staging of certification/credential language — Observations labeled with certification, credential or resume language are set aside with a note and not counted toward any marker surface. Canonical serialization pinned by SHA-256 digests (pure stdlib package) — Each read is a pure function of attempt, registry and review config, serialized canonically and pinned by a SHA-256 digest of reading and registry.

items.title: The Blue Line: A Stewardship Instrument for Maintained Commitments
items.summary: A stewardship instrument for maintained commitments: systems, obligations, and relationships to past work. It reads a declared file of commitments against a versioned registry and returns a fail-closed declaration-covera
items.content: The Blue Line: A Stewardship Instrument for Maintained Commitments Friedman, Daniel Ari Daniel Ari Friedman Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22833489 Friedman2026BlueLineStewardshipInstrument221 Active Inference Paper A stewardship instrument for maintained commitments: systems, obligations, and relationships to past work. It reads a declared file of commitments against a versioned registry and returns a fail-closed declaration-coverage verdict (MAINTAINED, NEEDS_ATTENTION, STALE, OUTSIDE_SCOPE) over the care signals each commitment requires. It measures whether the care a steward declared was fresh at the review date — never whether the care happened; a MAINTAINED verdict is not a warranty, SLA, availability guarantee, or proof of maintenance, and it never authorizes an action. License: Apache-2.0. See LICENSE in the repository. stewardship maintenance line set accountability An empty scan set (no matching commitment or unreadable file) returns OUTSIDE_SCOPE with notes and never yields MAINTAINED. The stated staleness-monotonicity property holds that the stale set is always a subset of the missing set. The verdict is a declaration-coverage statement, explicitly not a warranty, SLA, availability guarantee or proof of maintenance. The author notes the instrument only reads declarations and does not inspect repositories, run checks or contact anyone; the freshness window is a policy constant, not empirical. Versioned registry of twelve commitments with SHA-256 digest pinning — Commitments are frozen records (id, title, wire, tags, required care signals, kind) whose sorted canonical form is hashed and pinned in every reading. Staged, fail-closed intake normalization of declared files — Declared files are normalized; malformed tags or undated signals are set aside as intake notes rather than causing crashes or invented values. Freshness-window evaluation into MAINTAINED / NEEDS_ATTENTION / STALE — Required signals of tag-matched commitments are compared with signals declared within a freshness window (180 days by default) to assign a verdict. Formal definition of readings, commitments and fresh sets — A reading is formalised as a tuple and properties (fail-closed, staleness monotonicity, digest pinning) are stated. Worked examples: maintained quarter, stale repository, unmatched scan — Three illustrative declared files show the verdicts the instrument returns; these are examples, not an empirical evaluation.

items.title: The Violet Line: A Consent Ledger of Affected Parties
items.summary: A consent-ledger instrument for projects. It maintains a ledger of the parties a project affects and what they actually recorded at a review date; absence of consent is recorded — the UNRECORDED state — never inferred fr
items.content: The Violet Line: A Consent Ledger of Affected Parties Friedman, Daniel Ari Daniel Ari Friedman Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22833487 Friedman2026VioletLineConsentLedger222 Active Inference Paper A consent-ledger instrument for projects. It maintains a ledger of the parties a project affects and what they actually recorded at a review date; absence of consent is recorded — the UNRECORDED state — never inferred from silence, absence, or convenience. An executable review returns one of three verdicts (ACCOUNTED, UNACCOUNTED, OUT_OF_SCOPE); an ACCOUNTED reading never authorizes an action, a release, or a use outside the scope a party named. Subtitle: Absence of consent recorded, never inferred Apache-2.0 licensed; see LICENSE in the repository. consent affected parties research ethics governance In the worked interview example, one UNRECORDED moderator entry causes the review to return UNACCOUNTED, with absence recorded rather than inferred. Empty, fully set-aside, or unscorable inputs return UNACCOUNTED with a note rather than raising an exception or a fabricated value. No verdict, including ACCOUNTED, grants or implies permission; it describes ledger coverage only. The author notes the instrument cannot verify that a recorded state was given honestly, freely, or recently, and that ACCOUNTED is coverage, not safety. Per-project consent ledger with four recorded states — Defines a ledger of (party, state, scope, date) records where absence of consent is represented only by an explicit UNRECORDED state. Staged, fail-closed intake with set-aside codes — Intake dispositions every submitted record as KEPT or one of four set-aside codes with a preserving note, never dropping or inventing states. Tag-matched rule registry producing three verdicts — Versioned consent rules are matched to projects by declared tags and scored against the kept ledger to yield ACCOUNTED, UNACCOUNTED, or OUT_OF_SCOPE. Formal definitions and propositions bound to tests — States the instrument's behaviour as definitions and propositions (non-permission, fail-closed, declines persist, scope travels) linked to a claim-ledger test. Worked example reviews — Illustrates behaviour with a community interview study, a fully set-aside submission, and an out-of-scope project.

items.title: The Silver Line: A Memory-and-Succession Instrument
items.summary: A memory-and-succession instrument in the docxology line set. It reads a declared succession picture — what is preserved, what is entrusted to whom, what is allowed to lapse — and returns a verdict about declared provisi
items.content: The Silver Line: A Memory-and-Succession Instrument Friedman, Daniel Ari Daniel Ari Friedman Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22833485 Friedman2026SilverLineMemorySuccession223 Computational Paper A memory-and-succession instrument in the docxology line set. It reads a declared succession picture — what is preserved, what is entrusted to whom, what is allowed to lapse — and returns a verdict about declared provision and review gaps, pinned to a registry digest. A KEPT verdict describes declared custody at a review date; it is never permission and never a promise that anything survives. Subtitle: What is preserved, what is entrusted to whom, what is allowed to lapse Code is MIT licensed; see LICENSE in the repository. memory succession active inference declared custody review gaps On the worked lab-archive example, the reading returns NEEDS_PROVISION, while the empty-registry control fails closed. The formalism states that an empty scan set yields OUTSIDE_SCOPE with an intake note, and an unscorable registry yields NEEDS_REWORK with no findings. A gap on a lapse-accepted keepsake is treated as a declared release (NEEDS_PROVISION), not a defect. The paper limits verdicts to declaration coverage: it does not verify labels are real, judge quality, or guarantee survival. Keepsake registry with retention, restraint and lapse families — Declares kept items in a registry that carries restraint and lapse families alongside retention, so lapse is part of the declaration. Staged intake that sets aside malformed content with a note — Normalizes each declared succession item at intake; malformed content is noted and set aside rather than crashing or being repaired. Tag-intersection matching and present/missing evidence-label split — Matches keepsakes to items by intersecting tags, then splits each keepsake's required evidence labels into present and missing. Verdict pinned to ISO review date and SHA-256 registry digest — Each succession reading's verdict is tied to the review date and a SHA-256 digest of the keepsake registry that produced it. Worked example envelope: small lab-archive succession — Runs the reading on a worked JSON example with one declared record, a named custodian and a partial evidence set, plus an empty-registry control.

items.title: Coordinating the Field: The Case for Ecosystem-Level Technology Roadmapping and Community Working Groups in Active Inference
items.summary: Active inference is approaching a critical developmental juncture. The theoretical framework has matured substantially over the past decade, and applications are emerging across domains from clinical medicine to autonomo
items.content: Coordinating the Field: The Case for Ecosystem-Level Technology Roadmapping and Community Working Groups in Active Inference Ober, Edward Maren, Alianna Friston, Karl J. Hurtado, Ana Magdalena Pashea, Andrew Friedman, Daniel Sabine, Alexander Safron, Adam Edward Ober Alianna Maren Karl J. Friston Ana Magdalena Hurtado Andrew Pashea Daniel Friedman Alexander Sabine Adam Safron Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.23066903 Friedman2026CoordinatingFieldCaseEcosystem224 Active Inference Paper Active inference is approaching a critical developmental juncture. The theoretical framework has matured substantially over the past decade, and applications are emerging across domains from clinical medicine to autonomous systems. Implementations now exist in more than one language and institutional setting, and domain communities have begun to form. The field has not yet established a coordinated developmental infrastructure of the kind that has distinguished scaling fields from those that plateau. This paper reviews the historical record of roadmapping and working-group coordination across fifteen cases, and seven cases in which coordination gaps appear to have contributed to developmental limitations. Those histories are directly instructive for design. They show how independent convening, named objects of work, and public outputs have been associated with durable field-level coordination, and how the absence of those features has been associated with fragmentation, expectation-reality gaps, and delayed recovery. The paper proposes that community working groups, convened by the Active Inference Institute, are a useful and appropriate form for the next stage of that work. Year one forms the groups, agrees on a shared assessment framework, and runs initial assessments. Year two proposes domain roadmapping as the next step, decided group by group. The Field Working Group holds a terminology correspondence matrix, a comparison protocol for existing implementations, and the shared assessment framework. Domain working groups produce literacy materials, an initial self-assessment, and a published go/no-go. All interested parties are invited to the Charter Development Session at the Sixth Annual Applied Active Inference Symposium in November 2026. All updated information on the Call for Working Groups, Charter, Operating procedures, and more, are available at https://github.com/ActiveInferenceInstitute/Working_Groups/ . You can also access these documents on the AII website at: http://www.activeinference.institute/working-groups active inference free energy principle technology roadmapping working groups research coordination community governance Active Inference Institute
